assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, via the magic-wavelength trapping idea, combine thousands of atoms with Lamb-Dicke confinement and reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. That has redefined what can be measured: relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches and the coming redefinition of the second. The idea was original and the experimental demonstration is clean. This is exactly the kind of measurement advance that opens other fields.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and made the first demonstrations. Ye's group pushed the stability and accuracy to record levels and integrated it with frequency combs. Single-ion clocks and the comb are already recognized (2005), so a two-person prize for the lattice clock is coherent. Other contributors (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto, Schmidt's ion clocks) are not in the supplied credit, so some allocation ambiguity remains.
assessment.maturity: Many independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL and others) reproduce and improve the results, with clock comparisons across continents. The interpretation is stable and the work is mature and timely.
uncertainties: Priority relative to the single-ion clock and optical-lattice proposals by other groups is not fully resolved from the supplied text.
I have not verified the latest accuracy figures; they are from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Electromagnetically induced transparency and slow light are fundamental coherent-control phenomena. They underlie narrowband filters, quantum memories, and sensitive magnetometry. Harris's EIT and Hau's light slowed to 17 m/s are both clear experimental demonstrations that changed how people think about light-matter interaction. I know this area well from rare-earth-crystal slow light, so I weigh the evidence directly. Impact reaches applications.
assessment.attribution: Harris originated and demonstrated EIT with colleagues (Boller, Imamoglu, Field 1991). Hau's group made the dramatic slow and stopped light experiments in 1999 with Harris's concept. Imamoglu's role was in the early EIT theory and the 1991 paper; a two-name prize for Harris and Hau is cleaner, though crediting Imamoglu is plausible. Fleischhauer and Lukin on storage and stopped light are not in the credit list.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in atomic vapors, cold atoms, and solids by many groups for 25 to 35 years. The foundations are stable. Recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should recognize EIT itself or its quantum-memory offshoots, which have different contributors.
Allocation of credit between Harris, Imamoglu and others on the original EIT demonstration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry gives inertial, gravitational and fundamental-constant measurements of extraordinary precision, including gravimetry, measurements of G and alpha, and tests of equivalence principle. It is a flagship measurement technique with applications in geodesy, navigation and resource exploration. Strong fit to my own view that progress is limited by how precisely we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Bordé gave early theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer; Pritchard demonstrated the first atom interferometers with material gratings; Kasevich and Chu demonstrated light-pulse interferometers and gravimetry. Chu (Nobel 1997 for cooling) is not in the credit list, which makes the configuration slightly awkward but three names are reasonable.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across many labs and commercial gravimeters exist. Large-baseline and space tests are still developing, but the core technique is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with Chu's earlier recognition and absence from the supplied credit.
Whether a fair split can be made between the interferometer concept and its precision applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single NV centers in diamond gave room-temperature optical readout of single spins and nanoscale sensing of magnetic fields, temperature and strain. It opened quantum sensing in biology and materials, and NV registers have also served as qubits and quantum network nodes. Strong measurement-method and cross-field impact.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko did the first optical detection of single NV spins (1997) and coherent control; Lukin's group contributed nanoscale magnetometry and quantum register work. Other key contributors such as Hanson, Awschalom, Walsworth and Yacoby are not in the credit list.
assessment.maturity: Hundreds of independent groups use NV sensing and it is commercially present. Applications are still emerging and reproducibility of some in-vivo claims is uneven, but the core discoveries are solid.
uncertainties: Large number of significant contributors outside the three credited names.
Distinction between the single-spin detection discovery and subsequent sensing applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realized the Hubbard model, the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, and quantum gas microscopes with single-site resolution. This is a controlled quantum simulator, with precise measurements of many-body states. It is influential across condensed matter and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch observed the Mott transition (2002); Bloch and Greiner developed quantum gas microscopes; Esslinger realized the fermionic Mott insulator. Four credited names but a prize allows only three, so I choose the theory proposer and the two main experimental leaders. Esslinger and Jaksch are deserving but excluded.
assessment.maturity: Replicated widely and the interpretation is stable. Quantum simulation advantage over classical methods for relevant problems is not yet fully established, so some of the promise remains prospective.
uncertainties: Choice among four strong candidates for three slots.
Whether simulation is mature enough, or whether recognition should wait for decisive scientific outcomes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light reduces quantum noise below the shot-noise limit and is now routinely used in gravitational-wave detectors (LIGO, Virgo, GEO600), improving sensitivity. It is a clean example of a quantum resource applied to real precision measurement.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal for squeezed-state interferometry (1981); first experimental squeezing came from Slusher, Kimble and others in the 1980s; Schnabel led the GEO600 implementation. Credit is diffuse. I exclude Kimble to keep a two-person theory-plus-application structure, but the choice is debatable and Slusher, Wu and Walls are missing from the list.
assessment.maturity: Operational in kilometre-scale detectors; very mature and impactful. Priority disputes across many groups make a clean prize allocation hard.
uncertainties: Diffuse historical credit: Slusher, Walls, Yuen, Kimble, Vahlbruch and others.
Whether the prize would be seen as recognizing the technique or the LIGO application, already recognized in 2017.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Light-matter quantum interfaces, including quantum memories and repeater proposals, underpin quantum networks. I know the quantum-memory experiments in rare-earth crystals and atomic ensembles well, and the experimental road from proposal to efficient devices has been long. Concept importance is high.
assessment.attribution: Cirac, Zoller, Kimble and Mabuchi proposed quantum-state transfer between atoms and photons; Kimble's group built early cavity QED nodes. Experimental quantum-memory demonstrations also come from many other groups (Lukin, Polzik, Gisin, Longdell, Sellars, Kröll's own field) that are not in the credit list. Allocation is uncertain; I note my own field's involvement.
assessment.maturity: Quantum memories and networks are still maturing, with efficiencies and storage times below what repeaters need. Recognition may be somewhat premature compared with the lead candidates.
uncertainties: I have a potential personal stake in this field, so I place it lower to remain cautious.
Credit between proposals and demonstrations is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade enables programmable neutral-atom arrays for quantum simulation and computing, with tweezer arrays of hundreds of atoms and gate fidelities improving. Rapid and impressive experimental progress, strong measurement of many-body dynamics.
assessment.attribution: Lukin and collaborators proposed Rydberg blockade for gates (2001); Saffman did early gate proposals and demonstrations; Browaeys demonstrated blockade and developed tweezer arrays; others like Bernien, Endres, Ahn and Weiss are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Mostly recent, with demonstrations still evolving and error correction milestones fresh. Probably early for recognition compared with other candidates.
uncertainties: Maturity: field is advancing fast and the key results may be superseded.
Large set of relevant contributors outside the credited names.
